[[Incumbent]] [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Governor [[Bill Lee (Tennessee politician)|Bill Lee]] was elected to a second term with 64.9% of the vote, defeating his [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] challenger Jason Martin. Lee improved on his performance from [[2018 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2018]]. The [[Partisan primary|primary elections]] took place on August 4, 2022, with Lee and Martin winning their respective parties' nominations.{{Cite web |title=2022 Midterm Election Events Calendar |url=https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2022/politics/2022-midterm-election-calendar/ |access-date=2022-08-04 |website=www.cnn.com}}{{Cite web |date=2022-08-05 |title=Doctor critical of lax COVID rules wins Tenn. Dem gov race |url=https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-covid-health-nashville-memphis-2c940cf1573367bd12ad7e9ec5a4ffb6 |access-date=2022-08-05 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}} During the general election, Lee flipped reliably [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Haywood County]], home to [[Brownsville, Tennessee|Brownsville]]. It is one of only two remaining counties in Tennessee, along with [[Shelby County, Tennessee|Shelby County]], with a majority [[African Americans|African-American]] population. Haywood County had not voted Republican on a presidential level since [[1972 United States presidential election in Tennessee|1972]]. Martin won only Shelby and [[Davidson County, Tennessee|Davidson]] counties. This was the first time in state history that Davidson County did not vote for the winner in a gubernatorial re-election since Tennessee began allowing governors to serve for two consecutive terms. [[Voter turnout]] for the [[2022 Tennessee elections|2022 midterm elections]] in Tennessee was the lowest it had been in nearly a decade, with only 38.6% of Tennessee's [[Voter registration|registered voters]] turning out. This was far below the [[2020 United States presidential election in Tennessee|2020 presidential election]] in Tennessee, which saw a turnout of 69.3%.{{Cite web |last=McCullough |first=Erin |date=2022-11-11 |title=Less than 40% of registered voters in Tennessee turned out for the 2022 midterms |url=https://www.wkrn.com/news/tennessee-politics/less-than-40-of-registered-voters-in-tennessee-turned-out-for-the-2022-midterms/ |access-date=2022-11-11 |website=WKRN News 2 |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Gonzales |first=Tony |date=2022-11-10 |title=Tennessee voter turnout far below 2018 showing |url=https://wpln.org/post/tennessee-voter-turnout-far-below-2018-showing/ |access-date=2022-12-30 |website=90.3 WPLM News |language=en}} The last time turnout was this low in Tennessee was in the [[2014 Tennessee elections|2014 midterm elections]]. Tennessee's neighboring state [[Alabama]] saw a [[2022 Alabama elections|significant drop in voter turnout]] as well. Bill Lee was sworn in for his second [[Term limits in the United States|term]] on January 21, 2023, at War Memorial Plaza in downtown Nashville. In his inaugural address, he outlined priorities including transportation and energy planning related to the [[Population growth|state’s growth]], environmental issues, and reforms within the Department of Children’s Services, such as staffing and foster care and adoption systems. He also referenced workforce development through vocational and technical education and called for [[civility]] in [[political discourse]].{{Cite web|title=Gov.
